planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into deep, loose, well-drained soil in full sun; like its coastal cousin sea kale, this steppe-native crambe has a thick taproot and dislikes root disturbance, so choose its permanent bed before sowing.

directions: Direct sow into deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting the plant permanently since its thick taproot resents transplanting once established. Native to the dry steppes of Eastern Europe and Central Asia, Tatar bread plant produces a large basal clump of blue-green, cabbage-like foliage that can be treated exactly like sea kale — the young spring leaves and emerging shoots are cut and cooked as a potherb, with a flavor milder than cultivated cabbage. What sets it apart from other perennial crambes is its thick, sweet, starchy root: eaten raw in salads, cooked as a root vegetable, or dried and ground into a flour that was historically mixed into bread dough during lean harvests in Russia and Ukraine, which is the origin of the common name. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived, thriving on poor, dry soils where few other perennial vegetables persist, and require little more than an annual mulch of compost.
sources: Plants For A Future database — Crambe tatarica

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant divisions in spring into consistently moist, salt-tolerant soil in full sun; sea aster naturally grows in tidal salt marsh and does best in a low, damp spot that occasionally floods, though it also tolerates ordinary garden soil without added salt.

directions: Sow directly or set out divisions in moist, full-sun ground, ideally in a low spot that stays damp; sea aster is a short-lived but self-renewing perennial of European salt marshes now grown as a specialty vegetable, especially prized by Dutch and Scandinavian chefs under names like zeeaster or strandaster. The somewhat fleshy, narrow leaves and young stems have a pleasantly sweet-salty, mineral flavor reminiscent of samphire, and are harvested repeatedly through the season for use raw in salads, quick-pickled, or lightly steamed as a side vegetable. Unlike samphire, sea aster tolerates ordinary damp garden soil without true tidal salinity, though a light annual dressing of sea salt improves flavor and keeps the foliage tender. Cut plants back hard after their late-summer lavender-blue daisy flowers fade to encourage fresh basal growth and to keep the clump vegetative for the following year's harvest; older clumps can be lifted and divided every few years to maintain vigor.
sources: Plants For A Future database — Aster tripolium

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring and set rooted plants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Taunton Deane rarely flowers and is propagated almost entirely from cuttings, so a single sourced plant can supply an entire perennial kale patch within a season or two.

directions: Set rooted stem cuttings into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake young plants in windy sites; Taunton Deane is a centuries-old English heirloom perennial kale from Somerset, traditionally called cottager's kale for its long history in small kitchen gardens. It develops into a sprawling, thick-stemmed woody shrub that can eventually reach 6-7 feet tall and as wide, distinguishing it from the smaller, more upright Daubenton's kale, yet its leaves stay remarkably tender for such a large plant and are harvested continuously as a cut-and-come-again green. Because it flowers and sets viable seed only rarely, propagation is done almost exclusively by rooting stem cuttings taken any time during the growing season. Prune hard every couple of years to rejuvenate leggy stems and keep the plant productive; in favorable sites a single specimen can supply greens for a decade or more, making it a cornerstone perennial for food forest and permaculture kitchen gardens.
sources: Incredible Vegetables (Mandy Barber, UK) — Taunton Deane Perennial Kale
